title: Chronic pain: when pain stays
description: Chronic pain is pain that lasts for months or longer, such as long-term back pain. It is not imagined: it goes with real changes in the brain. The episode follows someone whose back pain did not go away, and compares them with someone whose pain did, or who never had it. One finding stands out: the brain's response to a painful touch looks much the same with or without chronic pain. What differs is how certain circuits work before pain becomes chronic, and how the brain behaves between pains.
caveat: The evidence comes from separate studies: one that followed people with recent back pain for a year, pooled analyses of how the brain responds to pain, and a study of people with chronic back pain doing a simple task. Chronic pain comes in many forms, and different types leave different traces in the brain, so this is not one pattern for everyone. An international expert group warns that brain scans cannot be used as a test for whether someone has chronic pain. The gradual loss of grey matter in people whose pain persisted is a change in tissue and is described, not drawn.

phases.name: Pain that lingers
phases.caption: Back pain that has lasted a few weeks. In people whose pain went on to persist, the nucleus accumbens, part of the reward and motivation system, was already more tightly linked to the prefrontal cortex than in those who recovered.
phases.typicalCaption: Back pain that has lasted a few weeks, in someone who goes on to recover. No unusual link is drawn.

phases.name: Becoming chronic
phases.caption: The pain persists. Over the following year grey matter decreased in those whose pain continued. That is a change in tissue, so it is described, not drawn.

citations.authors: Baliki MN, Petre B, Torbey S, Herrmann KM, Huang L, Schnitzer TJ, Fields HL, Apkarian AV
citations.title: Corticostriatal functional connectivity predicts transition to chronic back pain.
citations.quote: When pain persisted (SBPp, in contrast to recovering SBP and healthy controls), brain gray matter density decreased.

phases.name: A painful touch
phases.caption: A painful touch. The brain's pain response, in the insula, cingulate, thalamus and body-sense cortex, follows the same pattern as in someone without chronic pain.
phases.typicalCaption: A painful touch, in someone without chronic pain. The same pain response.

order.rationale: The pain-response findings come from separate experiments. Placing them after the pain became chronic is a way of presenting the comparison.

phases.name: Between pains
phases.caption: Doing a simple task. Normally the brain's resting network quietens during a task; in people with chronic back pain it quietened less, even though they did the task just as well.
phases.typicalCaption: Doing a simple task. The brain's resting network quietens, as it does in everyone during a task.

order.rationale: This finding comes from a separate study of people with chronic back pain at rest and during a task. It is placed last for presentation.

regions.explanation: Part of the brain's response to a painful touch in everyone. In people with long-lasting pain the overall pattern of response is the same as in people without it, and a pooled analysis of 266 studies found no difference in strength. Drawn the same in both.

connections.explanation: In people with recent back pain, a tighter link between the nucleus accumbens and the prefrontal cortex predicted that the pain would persist a year later. The authors take this to mean the circuit is involved in pain becoming chronic. The abstract says "prefrontal cortex" without saying which part; the line is drawn to the medial prefrontal cortex as an assumption. From one study.
